subChunks.title: Adolescent Development: Identity, Risk & the Brain
subChunks.hookHtml: Why do teenagers take risks? Why do intelligent, otherwise sensible 16-year-olds drive dangerously, use substances they know are harmful, or make impulsive decisions they later deeply regret? For decades, the answer was treated as a moral failure or a parenting failure. Neuroscience now offers a different account: the adolescent brain is a construction site. The prefrontal cortex — the seat of planning, impulse control, and long-term consequence assessment — is not fully developed until the mid-twenties. Meanwhile, the limbic system — emotional processing, reward-seeking, peer sensitivity — is in overdrive. The result is a biological system engineered by evolution for intense social learning, sensation-seeking, and risk-taking that our modern environment has not caught up with. Understanding adolescent development is not just academically important — it has profound implications for educational policy, juvenile justice, mental health, and parenting.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Biological Changes in Puberty

Adolescence begins with puberty — a period of rapid physical maturation triggered by the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal (HPG) axis, producing surges in sex hormones (oestrogen, testosterone, progesterone). Physical changes include growth spurts, development of secondary sexual characteristics, and maturation of reproductive systems. The timing of puberty varies substantially: early puberty in girls (before 8 years) and late puberty in boys (after 14 years) are associated with increased risk of psychopathology, body image disturbance, and peer relationship difficulties.

Brain development: MRI studies show that the adolescent brain undergoes substantial remodelling. Synaptic pruning — the selective elimination of underused neural connections — continues throughout adolescence and into early adulthood. Myelination (the insulation of axons with myelin, increasing transmission speed and efficiency) progresses from back to front, meaning the prefrontal cortex is the last brain region to fully mature. The resulting dual systems model (Steinberg, 2008) proposes that:

Limbic system (reward, emotion, peer influence):  Activated early in puberty
Prefrontal cortex (planning, inhibition, future):  Matures mid-to-late twenties

The temporal gap between these two systems explains adolescent risk behaviour.

Identity Development: Erikson and Marcia

Erik Erikson (1968) proposed eight psychosocial stages across the lifespan, each defined by a central crisis whose resolution shapes personality. The adolescent stage — Identity vs. Role Confusion — involves the teenager actively exploring and testing different identities (vocational, political, sexual, religious) before committing to a coherent sense of self. Failure to resolve this crisis produces role confusion — a fragmented sense of self and difficulty making commitments.

James Marcia (1966) extended Erikson's work by operationalising identity development as a 2×2 matrix based on two dimensions:

             Have explored?   Have NOT explored?
Committed:   Identity         Identity
             Achievement      Foreclosure
Not          Moratorium       Identity
committed:   (exploring now)  Diffusion
  • Identity achievement: Has explored and committed — associated with the best psychological outcomes: high self-esteem, resilience, and clear direction.
  • Moratorium: Currently exploring without committing — associated with anxiety but also intellectual openness. Often a healthy transitional state.
  • Foreclosure: Committed without exploration — typically to parents' or community's values without questioning them. Can be stable but brittle — vulnerable to crisis if commitments are challenged.
  • Identity diffusion: Neither explored nor committed — associated with the worst outcomes: depression, aimlessness, vulnerability to peer influence.

Peer Relationships and Social Development

The shift from family to peer relationships is a developmental hallmark of adolescence. Peer influence is particularly powerful because the adolescent limbic system is hypersensitive to peer evaluation (Crone & Dahl, 2012). Risk-taking increases dramatically in the presence of peers, even when adolescents know the risks intellectually. This explains phenomena like peer pressure without requiring the concept of 'bad influence' — the social reward signals from peers temporarily override prefrontal inhibitory control.

Dunbar (1998) proposed a maximum of approximately 150 meaningful social relationships that humans can maintain (Dunbar's number). Adolescent social networks, while intense and emotionally important, tend to be smaller and more volatile than adult networks, with more frequent renegotiation of status, inclusion, and exclusion.

Adolescent Mental Health

Half of all lifetime mental health conditions begin by age 14; 75% by age 24 (WHO, 2019). Rates of depression, anxiety, self-harm, and eating disorders peak in late adolescence. Risk factors include: genetic predisposition, adverse childhood experiences, insecure attachment, peer victimisation (bullying), academic pressure, and digital media use. Critical period for intervention: because the adolescent brain is highly plastic (still developing), early treatment of mental health conditions during this period offers the greatest potential for long-term recovery.

storyBeats.text: Dr. Chen shows a brain scan — two images side by side. 'This is a 14-year-old. This is the same person at 25.' The images show different levels of blue — the 25-year-old has far more activity in the frontal regions.

storyBeats.speaker: Dr. Miriam Chen
storyBeats.text: The prefrontal cortex — the part of the brain responsible for saying 'wait, what are the consequences of this?' — is not mature until roughly 25. That's not metaphorical. It's structural. When we imprison 15-year-olds as adults for decisions they made in peak limbic activation, surrounded by peers, with an immature prefrontal cortex, we are punishing them for a brain that science tells us was not yet capable of the regulation we expected.

storyBeats.speaker: The peer presence effect
storyBeats.text: Gardner and Steinberg (2005) gave participants a driving simulation task with and without peers watching. For adults, peer presence made no difference to risky driving. For adolescents, risky driving nearly doubled when peers were present. In a follow-up, the peer effect was still present even when peers were in a separate room and could only be seen on a screen — the mere awareness of peer evaluation was enough.

storyBeats.speaker: Dr. Miriam Chen
storyBeats.text: Marcia's model is useful clinically. When you see a young person who has never questioned the values they grew up with and is rigidly committed to them — that's foreclosure. When you see someone drifting with no direction and no engagement — that's diffusion. Both can masquerade as stability or as rebellion. Your job is to recognise the underlying identity process.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Maya is 17 and has recently started questioning the religious beliefs she grew up with. She is exploring different worldviews and spending time with friends from various cultural backgrounds. Her parents are concerned that she seems 'lost' and 'confused'. She hasn't yet committed to any particular set of values, but is actively reading, discussing, and thinking.

  1. Using Marcia's identity statuses, identify Maya's current status and explain your reasoning.
  2. Explain why Maya's parents might interpret the same behaviour differently from how a developmental psychologist would.
  3. Using Erikson's psychosocial stages, explain what developmental task Maya is working on and what a healthy resolution of this stage looks like.
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
1. Maya is in the moratorium status: she is actively exploring different identity options (religious, cultural, worldview) without yet having committed to a position. This is characterised by the combination of active exploration (questioning, reading, discussing) and the absence of firm commitment. Marcia associated moratorium with anxiety and uncertainty but also with intellectual openness — it is often a productive transitional state that precedes identity achievement.

2. Maya's parents are interpreting the absence of commitment as dysfunction ('lost', 'confused'). From their perspective, having settled values is a marker of stability and maturity, and questioning what they have passed on may feel threatening to family coherence. A developmental psychologist would interpret the same behaviour more positively: active exploration is the normative developmental path toward identity achievement. The discomfort of moratorium is typically preferable to foreclosure (committing without exploration) or diffusion (neither exploring nor committing). The psychologist would recognise Maya's behaviour as age-appropriate and healthy, though acknowledging that sustained moratorium without eventual resolution can become problematic.

3. Maya is working on Erikson's fifth psychosocial crisis: Identity vs. Role Confusion, which he situated in adolescence. The developmental task is to develop a coherent sense of self — vocational, ideological, and interpersonal — by actively testing and exploring different roles and identities. A healthy resolution produces identity achievement: a stable, internally generated sense of who one is and what one values, achieved through exploration rather than passive inheritance. Erikson noted that some degree of 'psychosocial moratorium' (a culturally sanctioned period of experimentation) was normal and healthy in Western societies that allow adolescents time before committing to adult roles.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: To what extent does neuroscience justify treating adolescents differently from adults in the criminal justice system? Draw on what you know about adolescent brain development, risk-taking, and identity formation. Consider both the supporting evidence and the counterarguments. Aim for 200–250 words.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
Neuroscientific research provides substantial justification for treating adolescents differently from adults in the criminal justice system, though important caveats apply.

The case for differential treatment rests primarily on the dual-systems model (Steinberg, 2008): the prefrontal cortex — responsible for impulse control, consequence assessment, and long-term planning — is not fully mature until the mid-twenties, while the limbic reward system is hyperactive throughout adolescence. This biological asymmetry is not a matter of insufficient life experience or poor character — it is structural. Additionally, Gardner and Steinberg's (2005) peer presence research shows that adolescents' risk-taking escalates dramatically under social observation in ways that adults' does not, further suggesting that adolescent criminal behaviour often occurs in neurobiologically heightened states that reduce the applicability of adult culpability standards.

Marcia's identity development model adds a further dimension: many adolescents who commit offences are in diffusion or moratorium states — without stable values or direction — making their choices less expressive of a settled criminal character than they might appear. Research also shows that the adolescent brain is highly plastic, meaning intervention during this period has the greatest potential for rehabilitation.

However, counterarguments exist. Brain maturation is a continuum — the prefrontal cortex does not suddenly 'switch on' at 25. Many adolescents show mature decision-making in low-pressure contexts. There is also a risk of applying group-level neuroscience data to individual culpability decisions unfairly. The most defensible position is that neuroscience justifies a presumption of reduced culpability and emphasis on rehabilitation for adolescent offenders, without being determinative in every individual case.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to your 16-year-old sibling why their brain is literally not the same as an adult brain yet — and why this should change how we think about teenagers making bad decisions. Use at least one real finding from psychology or neuroscience.

rabbitHoleTerms.description: The developmental process of eliminating underused neural synapses, increasing efficiency of neural circuits. Occurs throughout childhood and adolescence, with the prefrontal cortex among the last regions to complete pruning.

Steinberg's (2008) framework proposing that adolescent risk behaviour results from the temporal gap between early limbic system maturation (reward-seeking, emotion) and late prefrontal cortex maturation (inhibition, planning).

Marcia's identity status where an individual has committed to an identity (often parental or community values) without having explored alternatives. Associated with stability but vulnerability to crisis if commitments are challenged.

Erikson's term for a culturally sanctioned period during which adolescents are permitted to experiment with roles and identities before committing to adult responsibilities. Not all cultures provide this moratorium equally.

questions.questionHtml: According to Marcia's model, what characterises the 'identity achievement' status?
options: Having committed to an identity without first exploring alternatives
Having explored alternatives and then committed to a chosen identity
questions.correctAnswer: Having explored alternatives and then committed to a chosen identity
questions.explanationHtml: Identity achievement is the combination of exploration and commitment — the individual has actively explored alternative identities (vocational paths, ideological positions, relationship styles) and made a freely chosen commitment based on that exploration. This is associated with the best psychological outcomes: high self-esteem, resilience, and clear direction. It contrasts with identity foreclosure (commitment without exploration) and moratorium (exploration without commitment).

questions.questionHtml: True or False: Research by Gardner and Steinberg (2005) showed that the presence of peers increased risk-taking in both adolescents and adults equally.
questions.explanationHtml: False. Gardner and Steinberg found that peer presence dramatically increased risk-taking in adolescents (risky driving nearly doubled) but had little effect on adults' risk-taking behaviour. This supports the dual systems model: adolescents' risk-taking is particularly sensitive to peer evaluation because their limbic social reward systems are hypersensitive during this developmental period. Adults' more mature prefrontal cortex can better modulate the influence of peer presence.

questions.questionHtml: A 16-year-old shoplifts impulsively with a group of friends despite knowing it is wrong and having previously expressed strong anti-theft values. Which explanation is most consistent with neuroscientific evidence about adolescent development?
options: The adolescent is demonstrating identity diffusion — he has no coherent values
The peer context activated limbic reward systems in a prefrontal cortex that is not yet mature enough to override them
He is in identity foreclosure — his values were imposed rather than chosen
The behaviour reflects a stable antisocial personality trait
questions.correctAnswer: The peer context activated limbic reward systems in a prefrontal cortex that is not yet mature enough to override them
questions.explanationHtml: The description — impulsive action in peer context that contradicts known values — is precisely what Steinberg's dual systems model predicts. The limbic system's heightened response to social reward (peer approval, excitement) can temporarily override prefrontal inhibitory control in adolescents, producing behaviour inconsistent with explicitly held values. This is not identity diffusion (he has expressed values), not foreclosure (the issue is regulatory capacity, not identity structure), and not a stable personality trait (the behaviour is context-dependent and contrary to stated values).

subChunks.title: Adult Development Across the Lifespan
subChunks.hookHtml: For most of psychology's history, development was considered a childhood enterprise — the real work was done by age 18, and adulthood was just the extended plateau before decline. This view is wrong. Erik Erikson proposed that development continues through eight stages across the entire lifespan, each defined by a crisis whose resolution shapes how we live, love, and age. Modern longitudinal research has confirmed that personality continues to change meaningfully into late adulthood, cognitive trajectories in older age vary enormously by lifestyle and engagement, and the conditions of healthy ageing are not genetic lottery alone. Understanding adult development is essential for clinical work, occupational psychology, and any attempt to understand the humans psychology serves — most of whom are adults.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Erikson's Adult Psychosocial Stages

Following the adolescent Identity vs. Role Confusion crisis, Erikson proposed three adult stages:

Stage 6 — Intimacy vs. Isolation (Young adulthood)
  Crisis: Can I commit to close relationships, including romantic love,
  without losing myself?
  Resolution: Intimacy — ability to form and maintain deep, reciprocal relationships.
  Failure: Isolation — emotional withdrawal and shallow connections.

Stage 7 — Generativity vs. Stagnation (Middle adulthood)
  Crisis: Am I contributing something meaningful to the next generation
  and to the world?
  Resolution: Generativity — through parenting, mentoring, creative work,
  or community contribution.
  Failure: Stagnation — self-absorption and a sense of meaninglessness.

Stage 8 — Ego Integrity vs. Despair (Late adulthood)
  Crisis: Looking back, does my life feel worthwhile and coherent?
  Resolution: Ego integrity — acceptance of one's life, including its
  limitations and regrets.
  Failure: Despair — bitterness, fear of death, and regret at unlived possibilities.

Personality Development in Adulthood

The Big Five personality traits (Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, Neuroticism — OCEAN) show meaningful change across adulthood. Meta-analyses of longitudinal data (Roberts et al., 2006) show consistent patterns:

Conscientiousness    — increases steadily through adulthood (more self-discipline,
                       reliability, and goal-directedness)
Agreeableness        — increases, particularly in midlife
Neuroticism          — decreases (emotional stability improves)
Openness             — peaks in middle adulthood, then slowly declines
Extraversion         — slight decrease over adulthood

These changes are partially attributable to the social roles adults take on (parenting, employment) that reward conscientiousness and agreeableness — a phenomenon called social investment theory.

Cognitive Changes in Adulthood

A crucial distinction organises cognitive ageing research:

Fluid intelligence   — raw cognitive capacity: working memory, processing speed,
                       novel problem-solving. Peaks in late teens/early twenties,
                       declines gradually thereafter.

Crystallised intelligence — accumulated knowledge, vocabulary, expertise.
                       Continues to increase into the 60s and 70s.

For most everyday tasks, the wisdom and accumulated knowledge of crystallised intelligence more than compensates for modest declines in fluid processing speed — which is why experienced professionals often outperform younger ones despite slower reaction times. Dementia represents a pathological departure from normal ageing, not an accelerated version of it — normal ageing does not produce significant memory loss for personal history or semantic knowledge.

Ageing Well: Positive and Critical Perspectives

Activity theory (Havighurst, 1961) proposes that psychological wellbeing in older age requires continued engagement and active participation in meaningful roles. Research broadly supports this — social engagement, cognitive stimulation, and physical activity are all associated with better outcomes in late adulthood.

Disengagement theory (Cumming & Henry, 1961) proposed the opposite: that gradual mutual withdrawal of older adults from society is natural and healthy, a preparation for death. This theory is now largely discredited and has been criticised for pathologising dependency and legitimising the marginalisation of older adults.

Socioemotional selectivity theory (Carstensen, 1992) offers a more nuanced account: as people perceive their remaining time as limited, they shift their motivational priorities from future-oriented goals (meeting new people, expanding opportunities) to present-oriented ones (deepening existing relationships, emotional wellbeing). This explains why older adults often report greater subjective wellbeing and emotional regulation than younger adults — they have narrowed their social world to what matters most.

storyBeats.text: Dr. Chen asks the lecture hall a question: 'Who here has at least one grandparent over 70?' Most hands go up. 'Now — do you think their psychology, their inner life, their development, is basically over?' Silence.

storyBeats.speaker: Dr. Miriam Chen
storyBeats.text: Psychology spent the first fifty years of its existence treating adulthood as the destination — childhood development was the journey. Erikson changed that. His insight was simple and radical: there is no point at which we stop being in the process of becoming. Eighty-year-olds are still working on ego integrity. The questions that define us don't go away.

storyBeats.speaker: Crystallised vs. fluid intelligence
storyBeats.text: A 65-year-old chess grandmaster versus a 20-year-old computer science student with an IQ of 135 — who wins the chess match? Almost certainly the grandmaster. Their fluid intelligence (processing speed, working memory) may be lower. But decades of crystallised pattern recognition, tactical knowledge, and strategic wisdom built over thousands of games overwhelms raw cognitive speed. This is why experienced surgeons, judges, and architects often produce their best work in their 50s and 60s.

storyBeats.speaker: Dr. Miriam Chen
storyBeats.text: Carstensen's socioemotional selectivity theory is one of my favourite findings in all of psychology. It's essentially an explanation for why your grandparents seem happier and more content than you are, despite objectively having less time left. When time feels limited, you stop optimising for novelty and maximising — you start optimising for meaning and depth. It's a profound adaptive shift.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Margaret is 68 years old, recently retired from a 30-year career as a secondary school teacher. She volunteers two days a week mentoring young teachers and has maintained her close friendships but has declined invitations to join several new community groups and social media platforms. She reports feeling 'more settled' and 'less anxious about being liked' than she did in her 40s.

  1. Using Erikson's late adulthood stage, explain how Margaret's behaviour and emotional state might be interpreted.
  2. Apply socioemotional selectivity theory to explain Margaret's narrowing of social engagement without interpreting it as decline or dysfunction.
  3. Which of the two cognitive types (fluid vs. crystallised) would you expect Margaret to be relatively strong in, and why?
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
1. Margaret appears to be progressing well through Erikson's Stage 8 (Ego Integrity vs. Despair). Her sense of being 'more settled' and less anxious about social approval is consistent with ego integrity — the retrospective sense that one's life has been worthwhile and coherent. Her volunteer mentoring reflects generativity (Stage 7) that may be carrying forward into late adulthood. She does not appear to be in despair — there is no evidence of bitterness, regret, or existential crisis. The fact that she reports increased emotional stability suggests successful negotiation of the midlife generativity challenge.

2. Carstensen's socioemotional selectivity theory proposes that as people perceive their future time as increasingly limited, they shift priorities from exploration and opportunity-maximisation (characteristic of young adulthood) to present-focused emotional wellbeing and deepening existing close relationships. Margaret's decision to maintain established friendships while declining new community groups and social media is entirely consistent with this theory — she is selectively investing in relationships that provide emotional depth and meaning rather than expanding her network. Far from being disengagement or dysfunction, this represents an adaptive motivational shift that predicts greater subjective wellbeing. Research confirms that older adults typically report higher emotional satisfaction than younger adults despite narrower social networks.

3. Margaret would be expected to have relatively high crystallised intelligence — accumulated knowledge, expertise, vocabulary, and practical wisdom built over 30 years of teaching. Research shows that crystallised intelligence continues to increase or remains stable well into the 60s and 70s. Her teaching experience represents an enormous store of domain-specific crystallised knowledge. By contrast, fluid intelligence (processing speed, working memory, novel problem-solving capacity) would have gradually declined from its peak in her twenties, though this may be largely compensated for in most everyday domains by crystallised knowledge and efficient strategic use of mental resources.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Critically evaluate the view that cognitive decline in older age is inevitable and represents a straightforward deterioration of psychological function. Draw on research relating to fluid and crystallised intelligence, activity theory, and socioemotional selectivity theory in your answer. Aim for 200–250 words.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
The view that cognitive decline in older age is inevitable and represents straightforward deterioration is an oversimplification that conflates different cognitive systems and ignores significant variability and compensation.

Fluid intelligence — processing speed, working memory, and novel problem-solving — does decline gradually from its peak in the late teens and twenties, and this trend is well-documented across many studies. In this narrow sense, some cognitive change is a normal feature of ageing. However, crystallised intelligence — accumulated knowledge, vocabulary, and expertise — continues to increase or remains stable well into the 60s and 70s. For most real-world tasks, the wisdom and knowledge of crystallised intelligence more than compensates for modest reductions in processing speed.

Activity theory (Havighurst, 1961) suggests that continued cognitive, social, and physical engagement preserves function and wellbeing — supported by longitudinal research showing that sustained intellectual and social engagement predicts better cognitive outcomes in late adulthood. This implies decline is not inevitable but is partly lifestyle-contingent.

Carstensen's (1992) socioemotional selectivity theory offers an important reframing: older adults' selective disengagement from broad social networks and future-oriented goals is not dysfunction but an adaptive motivational shift toward emotional depth and present-moment wellbeing. Older adults typically report greater emotional regulation and subjective wellbeing than younger adults — hardly consistent with uniform decline.

Overall, cognitive ageing is heterogeneous, domain-specific, and partially modifiable. The narrative of inevitable, uniform deterioration is both empirically inaccurate and socially harmful in ways that may become self-fulfilling.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to your friend who thinks 'development stops when you turn 18' why psychology shows that adults — even elderly ones — are still changing psychologically in meaningful ways. Use one specific theory or piece of research to make your point.

rabbitHoleTerms.description: Erikson's concept of the middle adulthood drive to create something that will outlast oneself — through parenting, mentoring, creative work, or community investment. Its absence produces stagnation and self-absorption.

Carstensen's (1992) theory that as people perceive their future time as limited, they prioritise emotionally meaningful relationships over expanding their social network. Explains older adults' narrower but more satisfying social lives.

Cattell's distinction: fluid intelligence is raw cognitive capacity (processing speed, working memory); crystallised intelligence is accumulated knowledge and expertise. Fluid peaks in young adulthood; crystallised is stable into the 70s.

Erikson's concept of the resolution of the late adulthood psychosocial crisis: a retrospective acceptance of one's life as worthwhile and meaningful, including its imperfections. Its absence produces despair.

questions.questionHtml: In Erikson's stage theory, which psychosocial crisis defines middle adulthood (approximately ages 40–65)?
questions.explanationHtml: Generativity vs. Stagnation is Erikson's seventh stage, characterising middle adulthood. It involves the question of whether one is contributing something meaningful to the next generation and the broader world — through parenting, mentoring, creative work, or civic engagement. Identity vs. Role Confusion is the adolescent crisis; Intimacy vs. Isolation is young adulthood; Ego Integrity vs. Despair is late adulthood.

questions.questionHtml: True or False: According to socioemotional selectivity theory, older adults who spend time with a smaller circle of close friends are showing signs of social decline and dysfunction.
questions.explanationHtml: False. Carstensen's socioemotional selectivity theory specifically reframes this pattern as an adaptive motivational shift, not as dysfunction or decline. When time feels limited, people rationally prioritise emotional depth over social breadth. Research consistently shows that older adults who narrow their networks to close relationships report greater subjective wellbeing and emotional satisfaction than younger adults — the opposite of what a 'decline' interpretation would predict.

questions.questionHtml: A 70-year-old retired surgeon can still diagnose complex cases more accurately than many junior doctors, despite having slower reaction times on computerised tests. This is best explained by:
options: A ceiling effect in the computerised tests
The compensation provided by high crystallised intelligence (accumulated medical expertise) for reduced fluid intelligence
The surgeon's fluid intelligence has not declined because of her continued practice
Her greater Conscientiousness (Big Five) helping her compensate for cognitive decline
questions.correctAnswer: The compensation provided by high crystallised intelligence (accumulated medical expertise) for reduced fluid intelligence
questions.explanationHtml: This scenario illustrates precisely the distinction between fluid intelligence (processing speed, working memory — reduced in normal ageing) and crystallised intelligence (accumulated domain-specific knowledge and expertise — stable into the 70s). The surgeon's decades of medical practice represent enormous crystallised knowledge: pattern recognition, case-type heuristics, contextual knowledge of diagnostic probabilities. This knowledge compensates for — and indeed exceeds — the speed advantage of younger doctors with high fluid intelligence but less accumulated expertise. The fluid-crystallised distinction is more directly relevant than personality (Conscientiousness) or test artefacts.
